title: China-Russia Dashboard: Facts and figures on a special relationship
gist: A quantitative tracker of the China-Russia relationship shows bilateral trade rebounding to a record monthly high in July 2026 after a 6.9% fall in 2025, Chinese buyers capturing a ~19% discount on Russian crude in July 2026 (~USD 21.8bn cumulative savings since April 2022), dual-use shipments again above USD 4bn a year, and joint exercises shifting decisively naval. Cooperation is deep in commodities, payments and diplomacy but deliberately selective in the Arctic, in new pipelines and in rare-earth magnet licensing, where Moscow gets no favours.

insights.claim: China-Russia bilateral trade stabilized at USD 245 billion in 2024 — more than double the 2020 level — then fell 6.9 percent year-on-year in 2025 before rebounding in 2026, with July 2026 the highest monthly trade value on record.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The 2025 dip was cyclical, not structural — treat weakness in China-Russia trade prints as an oil-price and vehicle-demand signal rather than evidence of political cooling.
insights.quote: China–Russia trade stabilized in 2024 at USD 245 billion, more than double the 2020 level.
insights.locator: China-Russia trade has surged since Ukraine invasion

insights.claim: The China-Russia trade balance is roughly even in value with a slight Russian surplus but structurally lopsided in composition: Russia ships fossil fuels and raw materials, China ships cars, tractors, electronics and consumer goods, making the Russian side of the ledger hostage to energy price volatility.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Headline bilateral trade value is effectively a leveraged bet on crude prices; volume data, not value, is the cleaner read on the real relationship.
insights.quote: The value of Russian exports is thus particularly sensitive to volatile energy markets.
insights.locator: The trade balance has been relatively even

insights.claim: Since February 2022, mineral fuels — primarily crude oil — have averaged 70 percent of the value of China's imports from Russia, with base metals at eight percent, agricultural goods and foodstuffs six percent, other minerals five percent and wood and paper four percent.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Any sanctions or price shock that hits Russian crude hits 70 percent of Moscow's China earnings at once — there is no diversified fallback.
insights.locator: Russian natural resources in exchange for Chinese manufactured goods

insights.claim: China's exports to Russia are led by machinery and mechanical appliances at about 23 percent of value since February 2022, vehicles at 17 percent, electrical machinery at 15 percent and textiles, footwear and headgear at around 10 percent.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Chinese industrial and auto exporters, not commodity traders, are the listed beneficiaries of the Russia channel.
insights.locator: China’s exports to Russia are more diversified

insights.claim: Goods declared under simplified customs procedures (HS 98) — border trade and cross-border e-commerce parcels — jumped to around 12 percent of Chinese exports to Russia in June and July 2026, a second engine of the 2026 rebound alongside vehicles.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: A growing share of the trade is migrating into low-visibility customs channels, which degrades the reliability of official bilateral statistics and of sanctions monitoring.
insights.quote: A second driver is a sharp increase in goods recorded under simplified customs procedures (HS 98), including border trade and cross-border e-commerce parcels.
insights.locator: The rebound in 2026 has been driven partly

insights.claim: Chinese passenger car exports to Russia peaked above 1 million units in 2024 with nearly 70,000 trucks, then collapsed 42 percent for cars and 72 percent for trucks in 2025 as the market saturated and Russia raised its vehicle recycling fee and other protectionist barriers — though volumes stayed well above the pre-2022 baseline.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Russia is no longer a free growth market for Chinese automakers; Moscow is actively taxing the channel to shield domestic producers, capping the volume upside that underpinned 2023-24 export numbers.
insights.quote: The contraction largely reflects the market saturation as well as introduction of protectionist measures by the Russian authorities, aimed at curbing imports and shielding domestic producers from further declines in output.
insights.locator: A sharp increase in Russian imports of Chinese cars began in 2023

themes.theme: Energy flows and the pipeline chokepoint

insights.claim: Russian oil exports to China exceeded 108 million tonnes in 2024, roughly 30 percent above 2022, as Western sanctions forced Moscow to redirect crude eastward at a discount.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: China is now the structural clearing market for sanctioned Russian barrels; any Chinese pullback would be a far bigger supply event than incremental Western sanctions.
insights.locator: Fossil fuels are the backbone of Russia’s exports to China

insights.claim: In 2025 the volume of Russian oil shipped to China declined only modestly while its value fell sharply, a clean demonstration that price, not volume, drives the revenue Moscow earns from the eastward pivot.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Sanctions that widen discounts hurt Russian fiscal revenue more efficiently than sanctions that try to block volumes.
insights.quote: despite only a modest decline in volume in 2025, its value has fallen sharply
insights.locator: While China has become a key buyer

insights.claim: Russian coal exports to China hit a record in 2023 on sanctions-driven redirection from the EU, then declined and levelled out in 2025 as Chinese domestic coal output rose and import sources diversified — signalling a structural ceiling on this trade.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Coal is the first Russian export line to China to top out; expect the same domestic-substitution ceiling to appear in other bulk commodities.
insights.locator: Russia’s coal exports to China have grown steadily

insights.claim: Chinese LNG imports from Russia nearly quadrupled between 2019 and 2025 to a record 9.9 million tonnes, with the surge in Q4 2025 driven by China taking cargoes from the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 facility.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: China has demonstrated it will lift explicitly sanctioned LNG — a precedent that lowers the effective deterrent value of US project-level sanctions and adds hidden supply to the global LNG balance.
insights.quote: The staggering growth in 4Q 2025 is due to China’s willingness to import cargoes from the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 facility, showing its readiness to ignore the US sanctions regime.
insights.locator: Russian LNG exports to China have grown steadily

insights.claim: Gazprom pushed Power of Siberia-1 to 38.8 billion cubic meters in 2025, exceeding its 38 bcm nominal design capacity, meaning further Russian pipeline gas growth into China now requires entirely new infrastructure rather than utilization gains.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The existing pipeline is maxed out — every incremental bcm of Russian gas to China from here is a political decision in Beijing, not an operational one.
insights.quote: Gazprom indeed reached that level in 2025, exporting 38.8 bcm.
insights.locator: Russia began exporting pipeline gas to China in 2019

insights.claim: Beijing continues to withhold approval for the 50 bcm/year Power of Siberia-2 pipeline while Moscow pushes it, leaving the single largest potential expansion of Sino-Russian energy trade stalled as bargaining leverage.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: PS-2 approval is the cleanest single headline to watch as a proxy for how much pricing power Beijing is willing to concede to Moscow — and would be a material negative for LNG suppliers into North Asia.
insights.quote: So far, China has been hesitant to approve new projects while Moscow tries to push the project of the Power of Siberia-2 with its 50 bcm/y design capacity.
insights.locator: However, Russia needs additional pipelines

insights.claim: Disruption of Middle Eastern oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz in the first half of 2026 caused the value of China's mineral fuel imports from Russia to surge again, showing Russian barrels function as China's shock absorber for Gulf supply risk.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Gulf disruption is directly bullish for Russian export revenue into China — the two exposures are hedges of each other, not independent risks.
insights.quote: Following the disruption of Middle Eastern oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the value of mineral fuel imports surged again in the first half of 2026.
insights.locator: Due to falling global oil prices

themes.theme: The buyer's discount on Russian crude

insights.claim: China's discount on Russian crude splits into two distinct components — higher transport costs charged by intermediaries and a 'buyer's discount' arising from the bargaining power of the few remaining buyers — which move for different reasons and should be tracked separately.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Sanctioning the shadow fleet widens the transport component; shrinking the buyer pool widens the buyer's discount — different policy levers hit Russian revenue through different channels.
insights.quote: This total selling discount has two components: higher transport costs charged by intermediaries, and a “buyer’s discount” driven by the stronger bargaining power of the few remaining key buyers.
insights.locator: China has been buying Russian oil at a discount since Ukraine invasion

insights.claim: The buyer's discount on Russian crude for Chinese importers peaked near 18 percent in 2022, gradually eased, widened again in late 2025 after new US sanctions, briefly flipped to a premium in March 2026 during the Persian Gulf war, and reached roughly 19 percent by July 2026.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: New US sanctions demonstrably reopen the discount within months — the discount series is a real-time scorecard of whether sanctions escalation is biting.
insights.locator: For China, the buyer’s discount on Russian crude

insights.claim: Between April 2022 and July 2026 China's average discount on Russian crude was around 7.5 percent, worth an estimated USD 21.8 billion in savings to Chinese buyers.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Quantifies China's direct economic subsidy from the war — roughly USD 5bn a year of input-cost advantage for Chinese refiners that would vanish if the war ended and Russian crude re-normalized.
insights.quote: Between April 2022 and July 2026, China’s average discount was around 7.5 percent, corresponding to estimated savings of approximately USD 21.8 billion.
insights.locator: Between April 2022 and July 2026

insights.claim: The discount indicator is built from customs unit values on cargo arrival rather than spot prices, so it lags during sudden price spikes because shorter-haul Russian cargoes reprice before long-haul Middle Eastern ones — which is why it falsely showed a premium at the outbreak of the 2026 Gulf war.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Do not trade single-month prints of the discount during price shocks — the voyage-length artefact can invert the signal entirely.
insights.locator: Note: China’s percentage discount on Russian crude oil

insights.claim: The yuan's share of Russia's international trade settlements rose from under 2 percent before February 2022 to nearly 40 percent by January 2024, then stalled and has since fallen to an estimated ~30 percent, with the ruble's role increasing in its place.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Peak yuanization of Russian trade is already behind us — the CNY internationalization story via Russia has reversed rather than compounded.
insights.locator: The Chinese yuan share of Russian trade surged after invasion of Ukraine

insights.claim: The reversal in yuan settlement share dates precisely to the US Treasury's warning that it could impose secondary sanctions on third-country entities assisting Russia's military-industrial base, after which the Central Bank of Russia also stopped publishing yuan-share data.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Secondary-sanction threats on banks are the single most effective lever demonstrated against Sino-Russian financial integration — far more so than trade-level measures.
insights.quote: this growth trend halted after the US Treasury announced that it could impose secondary sanctions on third-country entities assisting Russia’s military-industrial base
insights.locator: However, this growth trend halted

insights.claim: Routing through third jurisdictions and alternative payment mechanisms now breaks the link between reported 'friendly-currency/ruble settlements' and actual yuan usage, so point estimates of yuan penetration are unreliable after the February 2024 data blackout.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Treat any confident number on CNY share of Russian trade published after early 2024 as an estimate with a structural break — the opacity itself is the data point.
insights.quote: the growing use of routing through third jurisdictions and alternative payment mechanisms dilutes the mapping between “friendly-currency/ruble settlements” and actual yuan usage, making point estimates misleading
insights.locator: Since official disclosures ended in February 2024

themes.theme: Military cooperation turns naval and routine

insights.claim: Russia and China have run 100 joint military exercises since 2003, 37 of them since February 24, 2022, with an all-time high of 11 in 2024 falling back to seven in 2025.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The count is a hard, published tempo indicator for military alignment — the 2025 dip argues the relationship is consolidating rather than accelerating.
insights.locator: Russia-China military exercises are now mainly naval

insights.claim: Naval drills and patrols now dominate Sino-Russian exercises — 22 of 37 since 2022, seven of 11 in 2024 and four of seven in 2025 — a sharp shift from the handful of annual naval events between 2009 and 2022.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The maritime tilt points the partnership at sea-lane and Indo-Pacific contingencies rather than continental defence — relevant to Taiwan and Arctic shipping risk pricing.
insights.quote: Since 2022, a large majority of joint exercises – 22 of 37 – have consisted of naval drills and patrols
insights.locator: Since 2022, a large majority of joint exercises

insights.claim: The 2024-2025 exercise cycle produced a series of firsts: the first joint naval patrol in the Arctic Ocean, the first joint coast guard patrol, the first joint aerial patrol entering the US air defence identification zone, the first joint submarine patrol in August 2025, and the first-ever multilateral SCO exercise in Iran in December 2025.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Each first expands the geographic envelope of joint operations; the SCO-in-Iran exercise in particular signals the partnership is acquiring a multilateral military format.
insights.locator: China-Russia military exercises peak in 2024, but decrease in 2025

insights.claim: The spring 2026 US/Israel-Iran war disrupted the annual China-Russia-Iran trilateral naval exercise, with no clear information on whether China participated — a sign Beijing hedges on visible military association with Iran under fire.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Beijing's rhetorical support for Iran is not matched by operational exposure — a useful discount to apply to any scenario assuming Chinese military backing of Tehran.
insights.quote: In spring 2026, the US/Israel-Iran war caused issues for the annual trilateral naval exercise involving China, Russia and Iran, with lack of clear information on Chinese participation.
insights.locator: In spring 2026, the US/Israel-Iran war

themes.theme: Dual-use flows, rare earths and reversed arms dependence

insights.claim: Chinese shipments of dual-use goods on the US/EU/Japan/UK Common High Priority List to Russia exceeded USD 4 billion in both 2024 and 2025, rebounding each time after sanction scares — in 2024 after the December 2023 US Treasury secondary-sanctions warning, and again through 2025 after an early-year dip.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Sanctions produce temporary air pockets, not durable suppression — Chinese exporters re-route within roughly two to three quarters, so enforcement announcements have a short half-life.
insights.quote: Chinese exports rebounded in the second half of 2024, suggesting adjustments to circumvent these restrictions.
insights.locator: Chinese dual-use exports help sustain Russia’s war effort

insights.claim: After China's April 2025 export controls on medium- and heavy-rare-earth items including magnets, Russia's shipments fell as deeply as other destinations and recovered more slowly, with licensing delays, customs scrutiny and the new traceability regime outweighing the 'strategic partnership'.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: China's rare-earth licensing machine is bureaucratic and non-discriminatory even toward Moscow — buyers elsewhere should not assume political relationships buy faster approvals.
insights.quote: There is no clear evidence of special treatment for Moscow: despite the “strategic partnership,” licensing delays, customs scrutiny, and the new traceability regime appear to have mattered more than geopolitics.
insights.locator: No special treatment: Russia’s slower recovery in China's rare-earth magnet exports

insights.claim: Russia's slower rebound in Chinese magnet imports was reinforced by weak Russian industrial demand, especially in automotive and other motor-intensive sectors, rather than by supply denial alone.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Russian industrial demand is visibly deteriorating beneath the trade headlines — a leading indicator for the wider Russian manufacturing cycle.
insights.locator: The lag was likely reinforced by weaker Russian industrial demand

insights.claim: China's arms imports from Russia have fallen steadily and in 2025 Russia accounted for a smaller share of Chinese arms imports than at any point in the period tracked, driven by Chinese self-sufficiency in military production and Russia's war-constrained export capacity.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The traditional Russian lever over China — weapons technology — has largely evaporated, removing a key source of Moscow's bargaining power in the relationship.
insights.quote: in 2025, Russia accounted for a smaller share of China’s total arms imports for the first time in the period under review
insights.locator: China’s dependence on Russian arms declines steadily

themes.theme: Arctic cooperation: real but deliberately capped

insights.claim: Sino-Russian Arctic cooperation is concentrated in energy and transport — the Maritime Arctic Transport joint venture between Novatek, COSCO Shipping and Silk Road Fund now routinely moves LNG from Sabetta to Chinese ports along the Northern Sea Route, with Yamal LNG the flagship of Chinese financing, construction and offtake.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Named corporate vehicles show where the money actually flows — these entities are the realistic targets for any future Arctic-focused sanctions.
insights.locator: China-Russia connectivity routes in the Arctic

insights.claim: Arctic cooperation stays limited because of a two-sided reluctance: Russia guards its Arctic as strategically sensitive and resists large-scale Chinese involvement, while Chinese companies are risk-averse about investing in Russia under sanctions and geopolitical risk.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate a Sino-Russian Arctic condominium from headlines — the binding constraint is mutual distrust plus Chinese corporate caution, and it is stable.
insights.quote: Russia has historically been cautious about large-scale Chinese involvement in its Arctic region, which it views as strategically sensitive. At the same time, Chinese companies have been risk-averse when investing in Russia
insights.locator: Despite growing interaction, cooperation remains selective and pragmatic

insights.claim: Flagship Arctic connectivity projects including the Polar Express fiber-optic cable and Power of Siberia II remain in planning or of unclear status, with delays tied to sanctions and financing constraints.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Financing, not politics, is the choke point on Sino-Russian infrastructure — watch Chinese policy-bank willingness as the real gating variable.
insights.locator: Several corridors are still in planning

insights.claim: China has no known military installations in the Arctic and confines itself to scientific research and resource projects while styling itself a 'near-Arctic state' and 'great polar power'; roughly half the Arctic coastline is Russian territory.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Chinese Arctic militarization remains rhetoric rather than infrastructure — a reason to discount near-term Arctic security escalation scenarios that assume a PLA presence.
insights.quote: China has gradually expanded its Arctic engagement. It became observer state in the Arctic Council in 2013 and describes itself as a “near-Arctic state” as well as a “great polar power”.
insights.locator: Arctic activities reflect Russia’s dominance and China’s selective engagement

insights.claim: Between February 2022 and April 2026 Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin interacted 19 times, Wang Yi and Sergey Lavrov spoke 33 times, and defence chiefs held 14 engagements — a cadence exceeding any other bilateral relationship for either country.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Meeting frequency is the most reliable published proxy for alignment intensity; a slowdown in this cadence would be an early warning of drift.
insights.quote: The frequency of these interactions surpasses that of any other bilateral relationship for both China and Russia.
insights.locator: China and Russia have expanded their bilateral relations

insights.claim: China-Russia voting alignment at the UN had been declining in both the General Assembly and the Security Council from 2018 through 2024 — most steeply after the 2022 invasion — but reversed and increased in both bodies in 2025.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The widely cited 'China and Russia are drifting apart at the UN' narrative reversed in 2025 — a measurable swing against consensus positioning.
insights.locator: China–Russia voting alignment in the United Nations increased in 2025

insights.claim: Beijing and Moscow now split roles in crisis messaging: after the US capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3, 2026, both presidents stayed generic and avoided naming Venezuela while foreign ministries and UN missions explicitly condemned Washington as a unilateral bully.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Read leader-level silence as deliberate optionality, not disinterest — the real policy signal sits at foreign-ministry and UN-mission level.
insights.quote: Chinese and Russian representatives also depicted the United States as a unilateral bully, using the Venezuela episode to present themselves as more restrained, law-abiding, and responsible great powers.
insights.locator: Beijing and Moscow align rhetorically against US actions in Venezuela

insights.claim: In the Chinese readout of the March 1 Lavrov-Wang Yi call after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran and the killing of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Lavrov is quoted offering stepped-up coordination through the UN and SCO while Wang Yi offers no matching commitment — an asymmetry the Russian readout smooths over.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Readout asymmetries are a cheap, public tell that Moscow is pushing for deeper coordination than Beijing will commit to — a reason to fade maximalist 'axis' narratives.
insights.quote: a forward-leaning coordination signal that is not mirrored by Wang Yi in the Chinese account
insights.locator: Notably, in the Chinese readout of the Lavrov-Wang Yi call

insights.claim: Russia's traditional caution about Chinese influence in the Russian Far East is eroding: border checkpoints are at record trade volumes, Amur River bridges have been built and checkpoint capacity expanded, indicating Moscow now prioritizes the Beijing relationship over old sovereignty anxieties.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Physical border infrastructure is a hard-to-fake, long-duration commitment signal — it locks in trade capacity that outlasts any political cycle.
insights.quote: suggesting Moscow is now prioritizing its relationship with Beijing, while becoming less concerned about China’s influence in the development of the Russian Far East
insights.locator: Checkpoints between China and Russia have become busier

insights.claim: Student exchange is sharply one-directional: Chinese enrollment in Russian universities rose from about 30,000 in 2020 to over 50,000 in 2024 (a 72 percent increase, 13.6 percent of all foreign students, with 16,411 master's students equal to roughly 36 percent of Russia's master's cohort), while Russian enrollment in China has only returned to pre-Covid levels.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: Human-capital flows run the opposite way to the economic dependency, seeded partly by Russia's cheap tuition — a slow-building channel of Chinese influence inside Russian institutions.
insights.locator: Chinese exchange students in Russia increase steadily every year

insights.claim: Tourism between Russia and China remains under a third of its 2019 peak of ~2.3 million Russian visits to China and over 1.9 million Chinese visits to Russia, with Chinese visitors at 5.8 percent of arrivals in Russia versus 7.7 percent in 2019 — showing the 'special relationship' has not translated into mass-level reconnection.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scobell
insights.so_what: The partnership is elite-, state- and commodity-driven, not popular — a useful caution against assuming deep societal ballast behind the alignment.
insights.locator: Russia-China tourist visits still not near pre-pandemic levels
